content: Burmese tofu, originating from the Shan region, is distinct from Chinese tofu, which is traditionally made from soybeans. Shan tofu is crafted using yellow split peas, while the Burmese variation is made from chickpea flour, also known as besan flour. The preparation involves mixing the flour with water, turmeric, and a small amount of salt, then heating the mixture while stirring continuously until it achieves a creamy texture. This mixture is poured into a tray to set, resulting in a firm, jelly-like consistency that is matte yellow in color and does not crumble when sliced. It can be consumed fresh in salads, deep-fried, or sliced and dried to create crackers for frying. The term pè bya refers to Chinese tofu in Myanmar and translates to beancurd in English. Fermented Chinese tofu, or stinky tofu, is called si to hpu in Burmese, likely derived from the Chinese term chòu dòufu. The yellow tofu made from yellow split peas is known as won ta hpo in the Shan State. To hpu gyauk, or dried tofu, is prepared by slicing yellow tofu into thin rectangular pieces and drying them in the sun, resembling fish or prawn crackers. The most common version of Burmese tofu, made from chickpea flour, is called to hpu or pè hmont. It shares the same yellow color and flavor as Shan tofu but is slightly firmer. Another variation, hsan ta hpo, is made from rice flour and is white in color. This rice-based tofu, popular in Shan regions, has a similar consistency to yellow tofu but a slightly different taste and is often used in salads. Fried Burmese tofu, or to hpu gyaw, is typically cut into rectangular shapes, scored in the middle, and deep-fried. These fritters are crispy on the outside and soft on the inside, often served with a spicy and sour dipping sauce or incorporated into salads. A variation called hnapyan gyaw, meaning twice-fried, involves cutting the tofu into triangular shapes and frying it twice, a traditional method in the Shan States. Another fried preparation, to hpu gyauk kyaw, involves deep-frying tofu crackers, which are commonly paired with htamin gyin (rice balls mixed with fish or potato) or served alongside glutinous rice, rice vermicelli in fish soup (mohinga), or Shan rice noodles (hsan hkauk swè). Green tea is the customary beverage accompanying these dishes. Tofu salads, or to hpu thouk, are a popular snack or meal in Myanmar. Fresh tofu, cut into small rectangular slices, serves as the main ingredient and is dressed with peanut oil, dark soy sauce, rice vinegar, toasted crushed dried chili, crushed garlic, roasted peanuts, fried onions, and coriander. A variation, to hpu gyaw thouk, uses fried tofu fritters as the base for the salad. Another form, to hpu nway (warm tofu) or to hpu byaw (soft tofu), is served hot before it sets, often garnished similarly to the salads. This warm tofu can be combined with tofu fritters or rice noodles in the same dish. Burmese tofu can also be prepared as a curry, known as to hpu gyet. In this dish, sliced yellow tofu is cooked with fresh tomatoes, onions, and garlic in peanut oil and fish sauce, then garnished with coriander and green chili. This preparation is a popular pescatarian option to accompany rice and is also favored by those who cannot afford meat or poultry. Besan flour, also called gram flour, is made from chana dal, a type of small, dark-colored chickpea commonly used in Indian cuisine. The rice-based tofu salad from the Shan States, hsan ta hpo, is as popular as the yellow Burmese tofu salad. Shan rice noodles (Shan hkauk swè) are often served with tofu fritters (to hpu gyaw) and pickled mustard greens (monnyingyin) on the side. A combination of warm Burmese tofu (to hpu nway) and tofu fritters (to hpu gyaw) in a salad offers a satisfying mix of creamy and crispy textures. Tofu salad vendors, such as those at the Kuthodaw Pagoda in Mandalay, are a common sight in Myanmar.
